title: Chapter 160: It's Real?!
html:
Once the woman was gagged again, the old man and Xu Tong settled down. Both seemed acutely sensitive to the word “hand,” as though it unlocked their darkest memories.

“Why does that word terrify them?” Chen Ge searched the room but found nothing connected to hands. None of the three prisoners bore an obvious injury, so the fear was probably psychological.

“What could have traumatized them this badly?” One possibility came to mind. According to Doctor Gao’s files, Patient Number 4 had lost a hand in an accident and developed phantom limb syndrome, believing the missing arm remained attached. His name had not been recorded—either forgotten by Doctor Gao or deliberately removed. “He is the only patient whose history involves a hand.”

Phantom limb syndrome was neither terrifying nor an especially severe psychological disorder, and medication and counseling could treat it. That raised the truly frightening question: why had a patient with such a seemingly harmless condition been confined in the Third Sick Hall?

What had he done to make the hospital classify him as dangerous?

Chen Ge returned to the young woman. Xu Tong refused to communicate, and the old man seemed incapable of doing so, leaving her as his only lead. He crouched beside the cage and met her eyes. Since ordinary conversation was impossible, he would try another method.

With a voice he was sure the woman could hear, he asked, “Did you see many hands?”

She gave no answer, merely shrinking farther away.

“Did you see a man with only one hand?” Before he finished, she began shaking her head violently, striking it against the bars again and again.

Her reaction answered several questions. The one-handed man was probably the source of her nightmares. Watching for the smallest shift in her expression, Chen Ge asked, “Was he carrying a weapon?”

Her eyes widened, and veins popped on her forehead.

“What kind? A saw? A knife? An ax?”

“Mmph!” The gag reduced her agitated cries to muffled noise.

“One of those, then. But what did he intend to do with it?” Chen Ge lowered his voice. “Chop? Saw? Did he call you imperfect creatures that needed correcting? Or did he want to borrow your arm?

“The number of victims has been shrinking, so you must have witnessed him ‘correcting’ someone. You saw everything, didn’t you?”

Veins stood out across the woman’s contorted face, and tears streamed down her cheeks. She kept shaking her head as if denying that she had seen anything.

“You truly know nothing? Then why does that hand frighten you? Did it fall beside you—or grab you when you tried to escape?”

However severe her trauma, its source remained etched into her mind. Flight from danger was instinctive; mentioning fragments of the event provoked involuntary reactions, allowing Chen Ge to infer the truth from her face and movements.

Instinct did not lie. Her responses had confirmed part of his theory. “Don’t be afraid. If you’re innocent, I’ll save you. I came tonight to expose everything and see these criminals punished by the law.”

Mildew saturated the laundry room. Chen Ge remained beside her until, whether or not she understood him, she gradually calmed. He reached into the cage once more and slowly removed the pillowcase.

Cowering behind the bars, terror carved into her face, the woman parted her lips and repeated a single word. “Hand… hand…”

“What could anyone have done to scar her like this?” Chen Ge set down the pillowcase. Behind him, something nudged the laundry-room door. The pressure was tentative, as though someone had tried to slip inside and unexpectedly met the washing machine blocking the way.

“This room is at the end of the corridor, and every nearby door is sealed. That wasn’t the wind.” He gagged the woman again, then glanced at the white cat half-buried in dirty clothes. Perhaps the overpowering mildew had ruined its sense of smell; this time, it had given no warning.

“I’ll have to rely on myself. Time to be more careful.” Mallet in hand, he watched the door. A hand slid through the narrow gap. Only several fingers could fit, probing the lock as though testing whether it still held.

“The real culprits are here.” Two Trial Missions had changed Chen Ge. Instead of panicking, he slowly opened his backpack and drew Doctor Skull-cracker’s fearsome hammer. Then he removed the wrist camera and set it on the counter facing the entrance.

The camera supplied the small window in the lower-left corner of his livestream. A glance at his phone would now show him everything beyond the door.

Preparations complete, he set the backpack by his leg, gripped the hammer, and concealed himself beside the entrance. Soon the door moved again. Whoever waited outside was losing patience; after several attempts, they rammed it with full force.

The washing machine toppled, and the door flew open. On his phone, Chen Ge saw two men standing in the corridor.

One had a twisted face and carried an ax stained red. The other had only one arm and held an iron shovel. Neither noticed the small camera aimed at them. The one-armed man nodded to his companion, then approached cautiously.

The toe of his shoe had barely crossed the threshold when wind roared beside his ear.

The instant the one-armed man committed to entering, Chen Ge swung the hammer. His timing was perfect. By the time the intruder understood what was happening, the hammer was already rushing toward his chest.

The monstrous weapon seemed to swell before his eyes. He raised his remaining arm to shield himself and flew backward several times faster than he had entered.
